# GM Assistant's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07

Toronto 19-5-0, 42 pts after 26 games.

## Role coverage

This phase asks whether Toronto have enough bodies at each role for the next three seasons, and which gaps the coach can plug internally versus which need a trade. The answer: scoring, speed, playmaking and clutch are covered in depth; checking is thin and aging; toughness is missing outright with zero players at 80+; and faceoff centres are a single-man show behind Sundin. Two of those three gaps cannot be fixed by shuffling lines.

**Toughness** is the structural hole. Nobody on 32 rostered skaters carries an 80 in the toughness grade. The best is Roberts at 73 (38 years old) and McCabe at 73 (29). Tucker, who the coach may want on the PK, sits at 70. Svehla is 69 at 35. This is not a line-assignment problem; the personnel do not exist. Every playoff series in this league has a physical test, and Toronto are built to fail it. Only an acquisition fixes this.

**Faceoff centres** are the second gap. Sundin 90 is the only centre above 80 in FACE. Richards is 70 at 24, which makes him a second playmaker, not a second centre who can hold the ice against top lines. Chlup is 75 at 18, a kid. Holden is 71 at 26 and not lined. The coach flagged this and he is right: behind Sundin there is no one whose draw win rate is a reason to dress him.

**Checking** at 6 players above 80 is thin but survivable for a year. McCabe 86 (29) and Fischer 82 (24) are in their prime. Upshall 80 (21) is a prospect. The problem is the other three: Roberts 86 at 38, Svehla 83 at 35, Tucker 83 at 29 and not lined. If Svehla and Roberts decline together, this drops to three. Tucker is the internal band-aid if the coach will dress him.

**Koltsov** is the clearest waste. Speed 92, age 23, 12 points in 11 games at 1.09 points per game, and the coach says he is being healthy scratched. The club has 25 players with speed above 80, which means there is no shortage of fast wings, but a 23-year-old producing a point a game who is not in the lineup is both a morale risk and a development stall. He needs to be dressed.

**Spacek** at playmaking 84, age 19, and not lined is the other development flag. The coach says he went from 16 minutes a game to scratched with no injury. If the club scratched a 19-year-old showing 84 playmaking, that needs a reason beyond a coach's preference. His stamina and durability numbers (79 durability) are not great, but he is 19.

**Goalies** are covered for this run. Belfour at 92/92 glove grades, 2.57 GAA, 0.907 SV% is still starting-calibre, but he is 39 on $6.50M expiring. Aebischer at 26, $0.50M, 3.00 GAA, 0.884 SV% is a real backup. Tellqvist is depth. No trade need here short-term; the summer question is Belfour, and that is already noted.

## Trajectory

**The trajectory question: can this club re-sign its own core, and does the 34+ payroll make the answer harder?** The answer is that the youth pipeline is deep enough to sustain three competitive seasons, but the summer 2005 cliff — 17 contracts, $28.6M walking simultaneously — is the entire dynasty challenge, and the four players aged 34+ eating $18.3M make re-signing the young core costlier than it needs to be.

**The age shape is not a cliff.** Fourteen players at 23 or under, eleven at 24-29, only three at 30-33, four at 34+. In five years, the 24-29 group becomes the 29-34 bridge and the youth fills in naturally. The thin 30-33 band is a one-season gap that fixes itself. The structural risk is not aging; it's the contract cliff.

**Gaborik** at $1.1M, 34 points in 26 games, 90 potential, one year left. He is the cheapest top-line winger in the league and the first player who must sign a 5-6 year deal this summer. Nash ($1.2M, 23 pts, 95 POTE, one year), Richards ($1.0M, 28 pts, 88 POTE, one year), Eminger ($1.2M, 11 pts, 99 POTE, one year) follow immediately. These four cost $4.5M combined today and will cost $12-16M on new deals. The $29.5M profit absorbs that comfortably.

**Kaberle** is the exception. At 26 with 75 potential and $1.9M, he is less a "lock up on potential" case than a "productive today, replaceable tomorrow" case. A 5-year deal is defensible at $2.5M but not urgent. Priority is below the four 95+ potential players.

**The 34+ group costs $18.3M for players in their last productive years.** Belfour ($6.5M, 39, 10 GP), Roberts ($2.7M, 38, 32 pts in 26), Svehla ($3.6M, 35, scratched), Mogilny ($5.5M, 35, 39 pts in 26). Mogilny is the hardest call: he has 2 years left so he cannot simply expire, and his production is genuinely good. But at 37 he'll be a $5.5M anchor with 55 potential and no market. The deadline is the window to move him while another club wants a playoff scorer.

**Belfour is the deadline asset.** $6.5M expiring, 39 years old, potential 50. The above-80 expiring mechanic works. Aebischer ($0.5M, 90 POTE, 26) is already the starter; Tellqvist ($0.8M, 91 POTE, 25) is the backup. Goalie coverage is solved at $1.3M. Use Belfour's contract for a first-round pick or a young defenceman.

**Draft capital is strong: two first-rounders (TOR's own and Detroit's), plus second, third, and fourth.** This is deadline ammunition. If the club buys at the trade deadline, the two firsts can acquire a top-4 centre or a second-line scoring winger without touching the youth core. If the club stands pat, they are summer picks that feed the pipeline.

**The move list, in order of consequence:**

## Calendar

**Are we buyers or sellers at the deadline, and what do we do with 17 expiring contracts this summer?** We buy. At 19-5-0, 42 points, first in the East with 8 of 15 making the playoffs, we are the clear contender. The deadline plan and the summer plan are one problem: lock the core, move the old money, plug the centre gap.

**Svehla, Roberts, Renberg.** Three veterans on expiring deals — 35 at $3.60M, 38 at $2.70M, 32 at $2.00M — that add up to $8.30M we should not carry into next season. Move all three before the deadline for picks. Any of them above 80 overall can be flipped for a draft pick using the expiring-asset mechanic. If they are below 80, find a club that needs a veteran blueliner or a left winger and take a late pick. Do not let them walk for nothing.

**Belfour** at 39 and $6.50M is the biggest single contract in the building. The read from the prior note stands: keep him through the playoffs, then offer two years at $3.5-4.0M or move him for a pick after the Cup run. At 39, a one-year re-signing next summer just re-creates this exact problem.

**Kaberle, Gaborik, Richards** are the three that cannot leave. Kaberle at 26 and $1.90M, Gaborik at 22 and $1.10M, Richards at 24 and $1.00M — all prime-age or near it, all cheap relative to their value. Each gets a 5-6 year deal the moment the season ends. Richards directly answers the coach's centre-gap flag: at 24 and $1.0M, he is the guy behind Sundin and he is about to walk.

**Nash** at 20 and $1.20M is the same story on a longer timeline. Lock him on a 4-5 year deal. The coach is already using him on the penalty kill, which means he is in the lineup.

**Eminger, Colaiacovo, Chistov, Upshall, Alexeev, Smirnov.** Six players aged 19-21 at $1.20M or less. These are depth pieces we should re-sign on 2-3 year deals, not 5-6. They are not proven enough for long term, but at those salaries the risk is minimal. Re-sign them cheap, develop them, and extend the ones who stick around year three.

**Holden** at 26 and $1.20M sits between the core and the depth group. He is the 2C we need behind Sundin if Richards stays at centre. Re-sign on 2-3 years. If we move him, we create the gap the coach is already complaining about.

**Tellqvist at 25 and $0.80M, Aebischer at 26 and $0.50M.** Both cheap, both young enough to develop. Re-sign both. The guide lost good goalies by forgetting. Aebischer at $500K is the best-value contract in the building.

**The deadline plan is two moves:** First, sign Richards to an extension so we are not trading from desperation later. Second, package Svehla or Roberts — whoever a contending club needs — for a pick and maybe a young prospect. We do not need to sell. We need to buy depth on the back end and clean house on the expiring money.

## League scan

**The question: who in this league fills Toronto's toughness and centre gaps, on a club that has a hockey reason to say yes?** The answer is that three players stand out — one is the best available asset in the entire league, and two of his peers sit on clubs that are mathematically rebuilding with expiring deals and no path to keeping them.

**Todd Bertuzzi** at VAN is the target. 95 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 29 years old, $2.6M, one year left. Vancouver are 14-8-2 with the lowest payroll in the league at $34.94M and $21.93M profit. They went zero rounds in the playoffs last year. A 95-overall player will demand $5-6M on his next deal; Vancouver probably won't go there. They trade him for a first-rounder and a rental rather than lose him for nothing in July. He fills the toughness gap AND gives a second line of scoring that the club does not currently have. This is the deadline move that changes the roster.

**Zden Chara** at OTT is the second target. 84 overall, 92 toughness, 93 checking, 98 aggressiveness, 27 years old, $1.7M, one year left. Ottawa are 10-10-2 with 11 expiring contracts. They are not a contender. Chara would want $4-5M next season on his next deal, and Ottawa has no interest at that price. He solves the toughness hole at the blue line and provides the best checking grade on the roster. $1.7M is nothing. A first-rounder gets it done.

**Shane Doan** at PHX is the third. 86 overall, 86 toughness, 91 checking, 28 years old, $2.4M, one year left. Phoenix are 9-13-4 with 14 expiring contracts and $47.81M payroll eating into only $14.26M profit. They are in a full teardown. Doan at 86 would demand $4-5M and Phoenix has $14.26M profit to spend on 14 replacements. He is a natural seller at this price and age. He fills toughness and checking on the wing alongside Bertuzzi if the club gets both.

**Kyle McLaren** at SJ is the fourth. 82 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 27 years old, $2.2M, one year left. San Jose are 9-11-2 with 14 expiring contracts and $20.71M profit. Same logic as Chara: a 27-year-old shutdown D at $2.2M expiring on a club that won't match his next salary. He is a cheaper version of Chara if the club only gets one blue-liner.

**Jason Arnott** at DAL fills the faceoff centre gap. 85 overall, 87 toughness, 80 checking, 30 years old, $3.8M, free agent after this season. Dallas are 15-9-1 and technically in the race, but their profit is only $11.47M against $66.88M payroll. If Arnott tests free agency they get zero. A first-round pick plus a cheap prospect is better than losing a 30-year-old for nothing. The trade crosses conferences (TOR East, DAL West), which removes the division-rival objection.

**Davison and Vandermeer** are depth pieces. Davison is 24, $0.5M, 86 toughness, 90 checking at SJ; Vandermeer is 24, $0.4M, 90 toughness, 88 checking at PHI. Neither moves on their own — PHI keeps a $0.4M player, and SJ has no reason to give away cheap youth. They are throw-ins in a larger deal, not standalone targets.

## Trade construction

**The question: what packages make sense to both sides, given what the coverage phase identified as thin and what the trajectory phase says we must shed?** The answer is three proposals ranked by certainty: Chara is the clean deal because Ottawa will sell, Bertuzzi is the big swing that fixes everything but faces a contending club, and Doan is the backup if Vancouver says no. None of them give a player the coach called thin.

**Chara** is the cleanest package in the league. Ottawa are 10-10-2, have 11 expiring contracts, and at $1.7M he will want $4-5M in July they won't match. A first-rounder plus a cheap forward body is market value for a seller moving an 84-overall blue-liner with 93 checking and 92 toughness. Holden is 26, $1.2M, not lined, 81 potential. They get a first-rounder and a depth forward they can keep or flip. We get the missing toughness on the blueline at 27 years old.

**Bertuzzi** is the move that changes the roster. 95 overall, 89 toughness, 93 checking, 29, $2.6M. Vancouver are 14-8-2, which means they might say no. But Bertuzzi walks in July, and Mogilny is 39 points in 26 games right now — elite production a contending team can use for the playoff push. Toronto sheds $5.5M over two remaining years of Mogilny's deal and gets the player who makes this team physically unplayable. The risk is VAN deciding this is their year.

**Doan** at 86 overall, 86 toughness, 91 checking, 28, $2.4M fills the same forward-toughness role as Bertuzzi at lower quality. Phoenix are 9-13-4 with 14 expiring deals and $47.81M payroll eating $14.26M profit. They are selling everything. A first-rounder plus a third is fair value for a full teardown to move a top-nine winger. If Bertuzzi doesn't land, this fills the gap.

**If none land:** Tucker has 92 checking and 88 toughness at 29, $1.3M, 3 games played. He is the internal answer to both gaps and should be dressed every night. Koltsov needs to be in the lineup. The toughness problem narrows from "nobody above 80" to "one player at 88" and survives the year.

# Coach's report — run 1, in-game 2004-12-07

Next game vs NJ on Tuesday 07 December 2004.

## Development opportunity

The question: is each young player getting the games and minutes his production has earned? The answer is mostly yes, but two kids are buried and one is sitting at home with nothing to show for it.

**Koltsov** is the loudest case on the sheet. 12 points in 12 games is a point a night, and he's doing it on the fourth line at 8.8 minutes. No fourth-liner out-earns that production by this much without a move. He belongs on the third line or better, and every game he spends on the fourth is a game of wasted development.

**Nash** is at 23 points in 26 games for 0.88 a night, playing 12.9 minutes on the third line. That's top-six production on third-line ice. He should be eating more of the game than he is — more shifts, not a different line necessarily. The chemistry point applies here: if the third line is clicking, give it more minutes before moving pieces around.

**Alexeev** is another 16 points in 26 games on the fourth line at 11 minutes a night. He's outproducing his role but the gap is smaller than Koltsov's. I'd watch him rather than move him tonight.

**Spacek** has 6 points in 11 games at 16 minutes a night and is now scratched. That production doesn't justify sitting. Something changed — I can't see why from here — but the scoresheet says he earned another look before the scratched label stuck.

**Safronov** is the structural problem. He's 23, POTE 91, a defenceman, and has zero games played. Klesla, Eminger and Colaiacovo are all under 22 and playing every night, so there's room in the lineup for another young D. Safronov at zero games means the club has a development asset rotting on the press box. I'd like to see him in the lineup, even in Colaiacovo's minutes if the two can rotate.

**Smirnov** has a POTE of 70 and zero games at 19. He's not being wasted; he's just not good enough yet. No concern.

**Chistov** managed 4 points in 14 games at 9.5 minutes and is now scratched. The production justifies the scratch. Fine where he is.

**Spezza** is the tricky one. POTE 99 but 11 points in 23 games on the fourth line at 9.1 minutes. The GM told me production drives the bus, not the scouting number. At 0.48 a night on the fourth line, the scoresheet says he's a fourth-liner right now. He stays there until the points say otherwise.

The rest are in the right spots. **Gaborik** leads the club with 34 points and 18.4 minutes on the second line. **Eminger** is at 15.2 minutes on the second pair. **Klesla** plays every game and put up 15 points from the third pair. **Upshall** at 10 points in 26 is a third-line winger, exactly what you'd expect. **Colaiacovo** at 18.4 minutes per game when he plays is getting top-pair minutes at 21 — that's a good sign, just inconsistent availability. **Chlup** at 18 years old is producing 10 points in 15 games on the third line at 11.2 minutes. He's earning every shift.

## Development trends

The window is 2 games wide, so no one's trend is settled, but minutes moved and those are decisions I made, not noise. Three players carry a signal worth naming.

**Chlup** is the one developing on schedule. 18 years old, 2 points in his last 2 games after 8 in his first 13, and his minutes climbed from 11.0 to 12.5. That 1.00 pace is a 2-game sample so I won't call it a breakthrough yet, but he's earning the next step. If it holds through December he belongs above the fourth line.

**Gaborik** is the one I'm watching. His season pace is 1.42 points a game — that's first-line production — but in the last 2 he has zero and his minutes dropped from 18.8 to 14.0. A 4.8-minute cut at 22 years old on a kid hitting at over a point a game is the kind of thing that stalls a player if it sticks. I did not intend to take his ice away; if this is the game script and not a plan, I need to put him back where he belongs. He's not stalling yet, but this is the week where it starts if nobody checks it.

**Roberts** is the one that should change the GM's planning, not tonight's lineup. He's 38 years old and his minutes just jumped from 16.5 to 22.0 while his production dropped from 1.29 to 0.50. At 38, 22 minutes a night is a number the body collects on eventually. The 0.50 pace over those 2 games says the legs are already slowing. The GM needs a plan for who carries those minutes when they come due, and it's not a problem that fixes itself.

The veterans Sundin and Mogilny both went quiet (0 points in 2) while getting more ice (16.9 to 19.5 each), but 2 games of zero is nothing against season paces of 1.46 and 1.62. No trend there yet.

No grade changes moved in this window, so everything above rests on production and minutes, and I've said as much about the sample size each time.

## Morale watch

The room is right. With Toronto at 14-2, morale has not moved on a single player since the last save, and nobody sits low enough for minutes to be the cause.

**Sundin** and **Mogilny** sit at 88, the lowest of the regulars, on 17.1 minutes each. If their calibre puts them in the 90+ band that means 20 a night, they're roughly 3 minutes short. But they're 33 and 35, the record is 14-2, and their morale hasn't budged — a 1-point grade hit from an 88 is tolerable. I would rather keep them fresh for a long season than chase 3 minutes a night into their legs.

**Chlup** at 82 is the lowest skater on the roster. He's 18 years old, 11.2 minutes a night, 10 points in 15 games. If he's in the 70-79 band, 11.2 is about right for him, and the morale drag is the results and the building settling around him, not his minutes. No change.

**Koltsov** at 12 points in 12 games on 8.8 minutes is producing at a point a game on fourth-line ice. Morale at 95, no movement. If he ever drops, I'm putting him higher. Not today.

The only sub-80 is Aebischer the backup goalie at 80, which is what a backup's life looks like. Tellqvist is at 96, so the crease isn't a problem.

## Role composition

**Sundin** at 86 faceoffs is the only centre on this roster who can actually win a draw. Richards sits at 72, Chlup at 75, and the fourth-line options at 52-53. That means we will be losing the draw to start every third-line and fourth-line shift, which puts our own defencemen under pressure they don't need. I cannot fix this with a lineup change; it is a roster gap that needs a second centre who wins draws.

**L1** is well-built. Sundin's 86 faceoffs and 87 playmaking centre Mogilny (88 scoring) and Roberts (80 checking, 70 toughness). McCabe and Fischer on the back end give us 81 checking on both defenders, so the top pair can handle the opponent's top line. No change.

**L2** is our scoring line and that is the right identity for a second unit. Gaborik at 96 scoring and 99 playmaking, Afinogenov at 88 and 89, Richards at 87 playmaking. The checking mean of 68 is thin but Richards at 91 best on the unit helps. The faceoff mean of 59 means Richards will lose more than he wins at second-line centre against the opponent's second line, but his 87 playmaking and 94 clutch make the trade acceptable. No change.

**L3** at checking mean 72 is the right tier. Nash adds size, Chlup's 75 faceoffs are the best we have at third-line centre. This is our shutdown third line and it does the job against bottom-six opponents. No change.

**L4** is the problem unit. Checking mean 56, toughness mean 54. This is not a checking line by any measure, it is three speed players (mean 88) with no structure. Koltsov's 98 speed is our second-best on the roster and he needs ice time to develop, but the line itself cannot protect him from a physical matchup.

**Koltsov** is at 98 speed and 53 faceoffs. He belongs on this line for development and he will improve his faceoffs with reps. Give him more of the game on L4.

**Tucker** is scratched with 78 checking and 67 toughness, third-best and fourth-best on the roster at those attributes. If he is healthy, putting him on L4 raises the checking mean from 56 to something near 65 and gives Koltsov a physical partner. The cost is one less speed forward, but we already have too much speed on that line and not enough of anything else.

## Opponent matchup

This is the night we find out whether 19 and 5 is real: New Jersey sits 14 and 2 and 3, 39 points, and gives up 2.9 a night, the best defensive number on the card after ours. Only one thing on the sheet changes for a matchup this clean, and it is the man in net.

**Belfour** starts. He reads 91 with morale 95 and has been behind a 10-game win streak; **Aebischer** reads 84 and is sitting at morale 80. Against NJ's skilled top six that is the whole argument. Matchup, not workload.

**Gaborik**, Richards, Afinogenov, and the Sundin line of Roberts, Mogilny, Sundin are the reason we score 6.9 a night. New Jersey has no line soft enough to justify breaking these up. **Friesen** (85 overall, 92 speed) and **Gomez** (82) are fast, but **Roberts** is 91 balance and 85 toughness and handles that, and our third line Nash, Chlup, Upshall is the heaviest front three we own and rolls to start and wear that top line down. That is a plan, not a change. The lines that won 19 stay.

**Colaiacovo** is the one small matchup trim. NJ's power play has 8 goals on 52 chances, more volume than we generate ourselves, and his penalty grade reads 55, the lowest on our blue line. Keep him off the first kill and lean on **McCabe** (89 penalties) and **Fischer** to kill against their top unit. One game, the kill chemistry resets tomorrow.

So: Belfour in net, the forward lines untouched, and Colaiacovo off the first penalty kill.

# GM Assistant's report — run 2, in-game 2004-12-04

Toronto 18-5-0, 40 pts after 25 games.

### calendar

## Analysis

We are buyers at the deadline. Toronto is 18-5-0 with 40 points, first in the East and second in the league overall (Colorado has 42 in 25 games). Eight teams make the Eastern playoffs and the ninth-place Senators sit seventeen points behind us at 22. There is no realistic path to missing the tournament, which makes the deadline question simple: buy the thing that will hurt us in round two.

That thing is centre. The Coach flagged it plainly — "thin behind Sundin, can't fix it by moving people around" — and the numbers agree. Richards is playing 16.8 minutes a night at 27 points in 25 games, which is a first-line workload for a second-line centre. Spezza is at 10 points in 22 games on 9.4 minutes, and Chlup is at 8 in 14 on 11.1. None of them can cover a top-nine centre in a playoff series, and the 57 games left before the deadline are more than enough time for a new centre to build chemistry.

The deadline target list is centres whose contract years show "1" — they are expiring assets whose clubs may shop them. Todd Marchant ($4.9M, 1 year), Alexei Zhamnov ($4.2M, 1 year), Jozef Stumpel ($2.6M, 1 year), and Yanic Perreault ($2.8M, 1 year) are the realistic range. Marchant or Zhamnov would be top-nine; Stumpel or Perreault would solidify the third line. Acceptance is uncertain — we do not know who will say yes — but the shape of the deal is right: for a team out of the race, a one-year contract on a 30+ centre is an expiring asset; we give a mid-round pick or a depth prospect, they shed money and gain a pick.

**On the summer, the problem is volume.** Seventeen players expire. That is not a summer plan, that is a fire drill, and we need to triage now.

**Lock up the core on long deals (5-6 years):** Gaborik (RW, 22, $1.10M) is the team's best winger and his salary is a joke — lock him for six years immediately. Richards (C, 24, $1.00M) is a top-nine centre earning rookie money; same treatment, 5-6 years. Kaberle (D, 26, $1.90M) is the top-pairing defenceman entering his prime; 5-6 years, likely a raise to $3.5-4M territory. These three are non-negotiable priorities.

**Lock up the youth on medium deals (3-5 years):** Nash (LW, 20, $1.20M) is the Coach's penalty-kill trust pick at age 20 — that says character and willingness. Four years at $1.5-2M. Eminger (D, 21, $1.20M) and Colaiacovo (D, 21, $1.10M) are young defencemen who pair with Kaberle for years to come; three to four years each. Smirnov (LW, 19, $0.40M) — four years at minimum salary, or let RFA rights hold him. Chistov and Alexeev (both 21-22, $1.10M) get three years if developing, or move one if the wing logjam builds.

**Short deals (1-2 years) for the aging veterans:** Roberts (LW, 38, $2.70M) has CHKG 90, TOUG 92, BALA 94 — still a presence — but at 38 on $2.7M, the game is ending. One year, reduced salary, or move him now. Svehla (D, 35, $3.60M) is still effective (ENDU 94, CHKG 92, ACCE 91) but his POTE 55 says there is no growth left and his age says decline. Two years at $2.5M max. Renberg (LW, 32, $2.00M) is serviceable depth at SHPW 88, PASS 88; one year.

**The Belfour decision is the summer's biggest single question.** His grades are still elite — INTE 97, GSH_ 92, GSL_ 92, BRKA 94, REBC 93 — but CONS is 50 and POTE is 50, which says he will not improve and his consistency is already flagged. At 39 with $6.50M expiring, he is either a two-year deal at $4M (accepting the decline) or a trade candidate now. The manual says to check goalies because good ones get lost to forgetfulness — but paying a 39-year-old $6.5M for one year while Tellqvist (25, $0.80M) and Aebischer (26, $0.50M) sit on the roster is the textbook "star on a yearly ratchet" trap. **Recommendation: keep Belfour for the playoff run, then offer two years at a reduced $3.5-4M. If he refuses, move him in the summer for a pick.** The "trade for a pick" mechanic works on any player above 80 whose future you don't intend; Belfour's core grades are all well above 80.

**The goalie backup question is urgent for the deadline.** Tellqvist at 25 and Aebischer at 26 are young and cheap, but neither has proven playoff reliability. If Belfour gets hurt in April, we are exposed. A backup goalie on a cheap one-year deal (or a young prospect goalie for a late pick) is the secondary buy target at the deadline.

**What I would NOT do at the deadline:** Sell. We are first in the East. The only reason to sell would be if we were retooling, and we are not — the young core is here and the veterans are winning.

At 18-5-0 this hasn't bitten yet, but in April, against a physical team in a seven-game series, this is the first thing that goes wrong.

**Faceoffs are a crisis behind Sundin.** He carries the entire column at 90. Richards, who is the second-line centre, sits at 70 — dead last among regular centres. Holden is 71 and not even in the lineup. The third-line centres aren't close. This means every defensive-zone draw outside Sundin's line is a coin flip at best, and a giveaway at worst. The Coach's flag is correct, and it cannot be fixed by shifting people around — the best available centre faceoff number on the roster is 71.

**Checking is thin and aging.** Six at 80+: McCabe 86, Roberts 86, Tucker 83, Svehla 83, Fischer 82, Upshall 80. Strip out Roberts at 38 and Svehla at 35 and you have four players barely above the line, two of whom (Tucker, Svehla) aren't even lined. Fischer 82 at 24 and Upshall 80 at 21 are the long-term answer if they develop, but right now this is a one-deep column on the checking wing.

On the Coach's specific points: Koltsov at 12 points in 11 games (1.09 ppg) with 92 speed is the best value player on the roster and must be dressed every night. Spacek's 84 playmaking at 19 with no injury reason to sit is inexplicable — put him back. The Gaborik PK move I support on principle (98 speed wasted on a defensive unit) but cannot verify Nash's defensive grades from the brief.

The only true acquisition target from this phase is a centre with faceoff ability — 80+ is ideal, 75+ is minimum, and a player who can kill a shift or two would address the checking thinness simultaneously.

### trajectory

## Analysis

Toronto's shape is, on the whole, the manual's target — seven veterans (30+), fourteen at ≤23, eleven in 24–29 — but the curve is top-heavy at the very top and the contracts are a single cliff. Four players sit at 34+ (Belfour 39, Roberts 38, Mogilny 35, Svehla 35) and three of them — Belfour at $6.50M, Roberts at $2.70M, Svehla at $3.60M — are on one-year deals. That is the right kind of cliff: the aging tier is priced off the books this summer, and we let it walk. Mogilny, 35, on $5.50M for two more, is the exception worth keeping — he's the team's leading scorer at 39 points in 25 games, and two years is the correct term for a veteran.

The dangerous summer is the same one. Seventeen contracts expire at the end of this season, $28.60M of salary, and the franchise core is tangled in that group: Nash (20, 22 pts, POTE 95, $1.20M), Gaborik (22, 34 pts, POTE 90, $1.10M), Richards (24, 27 pts, POTE 88, $1.00M), Upshall (21, POTE 99), Alexeev (22, 15 pts, POTE 94), plus defencemen Eminger and Colaiacovo (both POTE 99). These are exactly the players the manual says to put on 5–6 year deals, and they come up in one wave — the "all renew at once" trap, with several of them (Gaborik, Richards, Nash) coming off career-years that will ratchet their demands. Re-signing them is the single biggest trajectory decision this club makes; lock them early, before the market prices a 34-point, 22-year-old winger.

The money is not the blocker. Payroll $66.97M against revenue $57.01M with profit still $28.75M (the TV deal at $34.36M is carrying the books), attendance 17,408 at a $97 ticket. Re-signing the core will push payroll up — those kids are not staying at $1.0–1.2M on term — but the club has room, and letting the 34+ tier walk partly offsets it. The goalie transition is already half-done: Belfour is 39 on an expiring $6.50M deal, and Aebischer (26, lined, 13 GP) and Tellqvist (25, POTE 91) are both also expiring cheap, so we should not re-sign Belfour and instead settle the next two years in net. Draft capital gives us real ammunition for the coach's centre hole: we hold a first-rounder from Detroit on top of our own second through fifth, and at 18-5-0, 40 points, we are clearly in the race — so that first should buy a young centre we keep, not a rental.

### calendar

## Analysis

We are 18-5-0, 40 points, first in the Eastern Conference with eight teams making the playoffs. The gap between us and ninth (OTT, 22 pts) is 18 points with 57 games left. This is not a close call — we are buyers at the deadline, and the deadline is about 87 days out.

**At the deadline:** Buy for need. The Coach's flagged gap — centre behind Sundin and Richards — is the priority. Richards (C, 24, $1.00M) is also expiring, so a deadline acquisition at centre doubles as insurance: if he walks, we have a replacement. We should target a young top-6 centre with potential, not a rental. A first or second-round pick is the going rate per the manual. If the centre market is thin, a blueliner who can log minutes on the top pair helps too, since Svehla (35, $3.60M) is a rental we won't bring back.

**At the summer:** This is where the real work is. Seventeen players are expiring, and the list has a clean structure: a young core we must lock in and an aging/expensive fringe we must shed.

**Let go (4 players, saving $14.8M/year):**
- **Belfour** — 39, $6.50M. The manual says check the goalies, and here the answer is: he must walk. Tellqvist (G, 25, $0.80M) is the starter of the future at an eighth the salary. If Belfour is above 80 overall, try to move him at the deadline for a draft pick — the odd mechanic where 80+ players walk for picks applies. If not, let him expire.
- **Svehla** — 35, $3.60M. Keep for the playoff run at the deadline (he helps now), but do not re-sign. His minutes belong to Kaberle, Colaiacovo, and Eminger going forward.
- **Roberts** — 38, $2.70M. Same logic as Svehla. A useful fourth-liner for a cup run, not a roster piece for a team whose left wing is Gaborik/Nash/Koltsov.
- **Renberg** — 32, $2.00M. Expensive for a depth winger at his age. Walk.

**Renew on 5–6 year deals (6 players, $8.40M total):**
- **Gaborik** (RW, 22, $1.10M) — our best forward, lock him up long.
- **Nash** (LW, 20, $1.20M) — the Coach just moved him up the penalty kill, signalling he's a keeper. Six years.
- **Richards** (C, 24, $1.00M) — the centre the Coach says we need more of; sign him before anyone tries to take advantage of his expiry.
- **Kaberle** (D, 26, $1.90M) — our top defenceman. Five years.
- **Colaiacovo** (D, 21, $1.10M) — young top-pair D, six years.
- **Eminger** (D, 21, $1.20M) — same age, same role, six years.

**Renew on 3–4 years (5 players, stagger to avoid the cliff):**
- **Chistov** (LW, 21, $1.10M) — 4 years.
- **Alexeev** (RW, 22, $1.10M) — 3 years, gives us a look at whether he's a top-6 forward.
- **Upshall** (RW, 21, $1.20M) — 3 years.
- **Smirnov** (LW, 19, $0.40M) — 3 years, cheapest way to hold a prospect.
- **Holden** (C, 26, $1.20M) — 3 years, covers the centre depth the Coach flagged.

**Goalies (2-year deals):**
- **Tellqvist** (25, $0.80M) — 2 years, extend to 3–4 next summer if he takes over the starter role. This is the cheap insurance the manual warns about forgetting.
- **Aebischer** (26, $0.50M) — 2 years as third/backup depth.

**The clustering trap:** Nash, Colaiacovo, Eminger, Chistov, Upshall, Smirnov are all 19–21 and all expiring this summer. If I sign all six to six-year deals now, they all come up for renewal in 2010 simultaneously, and the payroll balloons at once. The 3-year terms on Chistov, Upshall, and Smirnov stagger the cliff so that by 2007 we're re-evaluating three of them with better information and the other three are locked in at young-player rates.

### league scan

## Analysis

The league scan produces a clear hierarchy. Toronto's three gaps — faceoff centre (best behind Sundin is Richards at 70), toughness (nothing above 73 on the roster), and checking depth (six at 80+ but Roberts 38 and Svehla 35 are the two best) — are all addressable by three players on clubs that are out of the race and carrying too many expiring deals.

**The best player on the board is Zdeno Chara.** At 27, he carries 95 checking and 94 toughness — he is the single answer to two of our three gaps simultaneously — and he's producing 31 points in 22 games at 29 minutes a night on $1.70M with one year left. Ottawa sits at 22 points, 8-10-2, with 11 expiring contracts and no direction. A 27-year-old defenceman on an expiring $1.7M deal is exactly the kind of asset a rebuilding club moves for picks and prospects. Our Detroit first-rounder plus a mid-tier prospect could land him.

**For the faceoff hole, the market offers two tiers.** The rental tier is Todd Marchant at 94 faceoffs, 96 checking, 30 points in 24 games, 20 MPG — but 31 years old on $4.88M expiring. Craig Conroy at 94 faceoffs, 89 checking, 25 points, 33 years old on $2M expiring is the cheaper version of the same thing. The keeper tier is Sean Avery: 24 years old, 93 faceoffs, 86 checking, 88 speed, $400K for two more years on a Los Angeles club that is out and carrying 13 expiring deals. His production is thin (3 points in 24 games, 12 MPG), but at 24 with those grades he is the developmental answer the Coach's flag points at. Eric Belanger is the value play — 97 faceoffs, $700K, expiring, 27, on the same LA club. He won't score but he wins every draw from the third line down.

**The one centre who blends production with faceoffs is Marc Savard at Atlanta.** 88 faceoffs, 86 speed, 84 playmaking, 24 points in 23 games, age 27, $1M expiring, on a club that is dead last at 13 points with 11 expiring contracts. He's the most productive faceoff-capable centre available and the cheapest. The risk is ATL may want a keeper's return for a 27-year-old even at 5-16-1.

I would not chase Pronger at $9.5M or Allison at $6.7M — both are on expiring deals with clubs out of the race, but the salary makes the return too high for what is essentially a rental. I would not chase Chara with a first and a top prospect; I would start the conversation with the Detroit first plus a depth piece and see what Ottawa wants.

### trade construction

## Analysis

Three proposals, ranked by how directly they fix what the Coach says we cannot fix by shuffling people around. The centre hole is the loudest flag — Richards sits at FACE 70, Holden at 71, and nobody else is close — so the first two proposals target that gap or the toughness void (zero players at 80+) head-on.

**First: Marc Savard from Atlanta.** He is the answer the Coach is looking for: 88 faceoffs, 86 speed, 84 playmaking, 24 points in 23 games at 27 years old on $1M expiring. Atlanta is dead last at 13 points with 20 expiring contracts worth $19.3M and $36.8M payroll against $34.4M revenue. They have all their own picks and no direction. A 1st rounder plus a high-potential young winger is the language a rebuilding club speaks. We send the Detroit 1st (which the trajectory phase earmarked for a young centre we keep — Savard qualifies at 27 if we re-sign him before market) plus Chistov (21, POTE 95, SPEE 89, 14 GP, $1.10M expiring) from our wing surplus. We lose a depth winger who has 4 points; we gain a second-line centre who produces at one point per game. That is the correct direction of travel at 18-5-0.

**Second: Zdeno Chara from Ottawa.** At 95 checking and 94 toughness, Chara is the single player who closes both the checking-thinness gap and the total absence of net-front toughness (our best TOUG is McCabe at 73). He's producing 31 points in 22 games at 27, on $1.70M expiring. Ottawa sits at 8-10-2 with 24 expiring deals worth $32.9M and no plan. Giving Klesla (22, POTE 97, 13 points in 25 games, $900K) plus our own 1st is a rebuilding club's dream return — a young top-pairing blueliner with a 97 potential and a lottery-adjacent pick. We still have Fischer (24, CHKG 90), Eminger (21, POTE 99), Colaiacovo (21, POTE 99) behind McCabe. This doesn't fix centre, so it's second.

**Third: Sean Avery from Los Angeles.** At 24 with FACE 93, CHKG 86, SPEE 88 and two years left on $400K, the contract is absurd value. But three points in 24 games means he plays a bottom-six role at best — he fixes faceoffs on lines three and four, not the second-line hole. We send Tucker ($1.30M, CHKG 92, 3 GP) and Holden ($1.20M, 0 GP), both surplus, both undressed, saving ourselves $2.10M in dead salary. LA is rebuilding with 13 expiring deals; a 29-year-old with real checking grades and a depth centre is worth more to them than a player producing 0.125 ppg. This is the cheap fallback if the big two fail.

**If none land:** The third and fourth rounds remain untouched, and Chlup (18, POTE 95, 8 points in 14 games, $2.34M for 2 years) could be developed into a 2C over the next 12–18 months. We are 18-5-0; we can win regular-season games without a second-line centre. But in April, against a team with a real 2C, the FACE 70 line gets buried. The deadline window is short; if Ottawa and Atlanta don't engage by early January, shift focus to free agents and accept the faceoff problem for this playoff run.

# Coach's report — run 10, in-game 2004-12-04

Next game at NYI on Monday 06 December 2004.

### development opportunity

## Analysis

The picture on our young players splits into three groups: those who are earning every minute they get, those who are not, and those who have no path.

**Earning it, no issues.** Gaborik (22) has 34 points in 25 games at 18.4 minutes a night on the second line — he's the best player on the roster among the under-24 group and plays like it. Nash (20) is 25 and 25 with 22 points and 12.9 minutes on the third line, exactly where a 20-year-old should be. Klesla (22) at 13 points and 14.7 minutes every night, Eminger (21) at 10 points and 15.0 minutes on the third defensive pair, Upshall (21) at 10 points and 13.5 minutes on the right side of the third line — all grinding, all in the lineup, all fine. Colaiacovo (21) is at 10 games and 18.7 minutes on the second pair, and that low GP is injury, not neglect. He's back and playing.

**Koltsov is the problem.** Twelve points in eleven games. That's 1.09 a night, the best rate on the club, and he's on the fourth line at 9.3 minutes. Alexeev, his line-mate, has 15 points in 25 games (0.60 ppg) and plays every night. Koltsov is 23 — he's not a project who needs to wait his turn, he's a young man producing at a first-line rate on the fourth line and sitting out fourteen of twenty-five games. The decision made earlier today to give his line more of the game is right, but that addresses the ice time, not the games played. He needs to be dressed every night. If he's healthy, there is no argument.

**Spacek is a question I cannot answer.** Eleven games at 16 minutes a night at 19, potential 91, and then he simply vanished from the dressing list. No injury row. He went from a regular third-liner to a scratch and nobody can tell me why. At 19, sixteen minutes a game is his band, and losing that with no apparent reason is the kind of thing that turns a promising centre into a confused one. I need to understand what happened and get him back in.

**Chistov has not earned it.** Four points in fourteen games at 9.5 minutes. Potential 95 is a scouting opinion, not a production number. He's 21, healthy, and producing less than half a point a game on bottom-six minutes. He was barely getting enough to develop when he was playing, and now he's out. I feel for the kid, but the numbers say he hasn't done enough to displace Nash, Koltsov, or anyone ahead of him. If he's going to break out, it may need a bigger role — but I'm not going to give a top-nine spot to a guy with 0.29 points a game.

**Chlup is fine for 18.** Fourteen games, 11.1 minutes, eight points on the third line. His morale at 82 is the lowest in the group, which bears watching but isn't alarming — he's a rookie centre at 18 on a winning team. No change needed, just keep an eye on that number.

**Safronov and Smirnov have no path.** Safronov (23, potential 91) has zero games with Colaiacovo back on the second pair, Klesla and Eminger every night ahead of him. There are four defencemen in front of him and the seventh slot goes to Svehla for the penalty kills. Smirnov (19, potential 70) has zero games and zero production and the lowest potential in the group. Neither is being wasted — they're behind people who are playing better hockey.

### morale watch

## Analysis

The room is right. Every man on the sheet is holding steady — the `chg` column is `=` top to bottom — and morale runs 80 to 100. Nobody is slipping, so there is no morale fire to put out Monday night in Long Island. That lets me leave the lines alone and play for the matchup, not to fix the room.

The one number worth naming is the floor: Aebischer at 80. He's our backup, dressed, 13 starts. That's not a minutes grievance I can fix with a line — a backup goalie gets what the starter gives him, and Belfour is playing 56.0 a night when he's in. If Aebischer starts sliding from here it's about his role and our results, not about who wings a line. I'll watch it; it's not a decision today.

The one forward carrying a calibre-versus-minutes mismatch is still Koltsov — 12 points in 11 games at 9.3 a night on the fourth line, that's the best points-per-game on the club. But his morale is 95 and unmoved, so this has never been a happiness problem; it's a "use our best player" problem, and that's the development/production ask I've already flagged (give the Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev line more of the game). I'm not reaching for it as a morale fix, because morale isn't broken there.

On the other side of the ledger — a depth man over his head — I see nobody. Alexeev 25 games at 11.3 on the fourth line, Upshall 13.5, Eminger 15.0, Klesla 14.7 — all young guys at sensible minutes for their role, no one drowning. Sundin sits at 16.9, which for a centre of his grade is a shade light against a 20 a night, but he's at 88 and steady, and I'm not tearing apart the line that's carrying our offence to claw back two minutes.

Bottom line: no morale-driven change for NYI. The lines go out as they are.

### role composition

## Analysis

Start with what fits, because most of this is fine. The first line is built right: Sundin and Mogilny are the scoring engine (scoring 87 mean, 95 best; Mogilny 94 scoring, 92 clutch) with Roberts and McCabe in front of them — two 86-checking, 73-toughness defencemen who give L1 a real shutdown spine without losing the top-end offence. Don't touch it. The second line is a pure speed/scoring unit — Gaborik 98 speed, Afinogenov 96, Richards taking the 70 faceoff — built to run, not to grind. That's an arrangement choice I'm content with as long as I don't roll it out against the opponent's top line. The third line is the one I want to point at: Chlup, Upshall, Nash, Eminger, Klesla carry the **highest checking mean of any forward line at 79** (Nash is the power body in there), and Chlup takes the 75 draws. That's a properly constructed checking line. Leave all three even-strength units alone.

The role-fit problem is on the penalty kill. K1 is Roberts, Colaiacovo, Gaborik, Fischer — and Gaborik is a 92-scoring, 98-speed winger killing penalties. His skill is not the one this unit needs; the unit's job is checking (it sits at 77 mean, and Roberts 86 and Fischer do that work). Pulling Gaborik off the kill is a small move — it doesn't disturb any even-strength line or the power play — and I replace him with **Nash**, who already lives on that third checking line and is the natural body for the shift. This frees Gaborik's legs for offence and matches the unit's purpose to its personnel. It's the same call I flagged about Gaborik's special-teams misuse; this fixes it.

Fourth line stays a speed line on purpose (Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev: 88 mean speed, 60 checking) — that's by design, not a gap; making it check isn't the job.

What I *can't* fix with a lineup is the draws. At centre we are Sundin at 90 and then a cliff — Chlup 75 (and he's 18), Richards 70, Holden 71 scratched. Behind Sundin nobody wins a clean faceoff. That is a roster thinness, not an arrangement problem, and against a strong faceoff club it costs us zone starts we'll never get back.

### opponent matchup

## Analysis

This is a mismatch on paper and I'm not going to manufacture one on the bench. They're 12-10-1, 95 goals for and 91 against — **2.50 a night scored, 3.30 allowed** (brief). We're 18-5 on ten straight wins at 7.50 for, 1.80 against. The single loudest number on the sheet is their power play: **2 goals in 57 chances, 3.5%** (brief). Aucoin carries a 96 shot power and Hamrlik 93, so the cannon is there — it just can't get the puck in the net on the man advantage.

That kills the one matchup change I was saving. My checker-redress plan was explicitly to load the Tucker (CHKG 92) / Fischer (CHKG 90) / Svehla units against a hot offensive club. **This is the opposite** — a 2.5-goal-a-night team, dead on the power play, and my own note says their best scorer (Yashin, 25 in 16) isn't even in their lineup right now. Respect a PP that can't score? No. So the checking surplus stays holstered for a game that actually calls for it. The only real threat is their first line — Bates (SPEE 93, FACE 94), Kvasha (BALA 93, TOUG 75), Parrish (CHKG 85, SHPW 89) — fast and heavy. Sundin (FACE 90) already draws the 94 faceoff man; that's covered and I won't reshuffle a 10-game heater to chase one line on a team that allows 3.3 a game.

So: **no change for this opponent.** The two things that *are* moving Monday — Belfour in net (returns 12-05, our rest/development rotation) and Gaborik onto the first power-play unit (his role, not their problem) — stand, but I'm flagging them because they carry their own reasons. Neither is a read on *this* team; don't let me or you mistake them for matchup chess. We play our game.

# Coach's report — run 8, in-game 2004-12-04

Next game at NYI on Monday 06 December 2004.

### development opportunity

## Analysis

The well-used group is settled and good: Nash, Gaborik, Eminger, Upshall, Klesla and Alexeev are all in every game or close to it, logging real minutes at their tier. Colaiacovo is back on the second pair at 18.7 minutes a night when he plays and his minutes-per-game is right for a young top-four defenceman. No touch needed there.

Koltsov is the one the fourth-line decision targets — 1.09 points per game, best on the club, and still stuck at 11 games and 9.3 minutes a night. The decision was made last activation to give that line more of the game, and it hasn't taken hold yet. I need to see his GP climb over the next stretch or the fourth line needs a roster move to create space for him. No new change today; I'm watching whether the existing call sticks.

Spacek is the new concern. A 19-year-old centre with a 91 scouting number who was logging 16 minutes a night has dropped off the dressing list with no injury. That's exactly the position where we have a cliff — below Sundin, there's nobody else who takes draws until Chlup, who's 18. Spacek was earning his spot and is now sitting. I don't know why he came out, and I want him back in the lineup.

Chlup's morale at 82 is the lowest of any young player on the club. He's an 18-year-old on the third line getting 11 minutes — that's fair usage, and the morale dip is small. Keep him in the lineup, keep the third line together, and if the team's results hold his number should recover on its own. No intervention needed beyond playing him.

Chistov is healthy, out of the lineup, and has four points in 14 games. The scouting number is 95, but what he's produced doesn't demand a spot right now. I'm not putting him back in until he shows more at practice or someone needs rest.

Safronov and Smirnov: plain speech. Safronov is 23, a defenceman, zero games, and with Colaiacovo locked into the second pair there is no path to ice time here. He's wasting on the roster. Smirnov is 19 with a 70 scouting number — the lowest on the young list by a wide margin — and zero games. He's not worth a roster spot at this level today. Both are the GM's decisions, not mine, but I'm raising them.

### role composition

## Analysis

The lines are mostly well-built. First line has everything — Sundin wins draws, Roberts and Fischer check at 86, Mogilny scores at 94, McCabe adds toughness. Second line is the speed line by design, Gaborik and Afinogenov at 98 and 96 speed give it an identity, and Richards at 70 is the best draw-taker available for that centre spot anyway. Third line is solid two-way with Chlup at 75 in the middle. Fourth line is speed, which is what I decided on December 4th. No reason to touch any of those.

The problem is **K1**. Gaborik is still on the first penalty-kill unit with a 92-scoring, 98-speed profile and checking that isn't in the elite tier. Tucker is sitting at 83 checking in the press box, doing nothing. I already made this call last run — it hasn't been applied yet. Tucker comes onto K1, Gaborik comes off. Same with Svehla: 83 checking, 94 stamina, currently scratched. He should be dressed as the seventh defenceman and onto the kill.

On the faceoff question: this is a genuine roster gap, not a lineup problem. Sundin at 90 is the only quality draw-taker. Chlup at 75 is a teenager still growing into the role, Richards tops out at 70, and Holden at 71 is scratched. Against strong centres on the road, lines two through four are getting beat at the dot every night. No rearrangement of this roster fixes it. That's a trade-deadline conversation, not a lineup conversation.

Everything else is fine as it stands.

### opponent matchup

## Analysis

This is not a game to over-coach. New York scores 2.5 a night and lets in 3.3 — a bottom-half club on a wobbly run (WWLLLLLWWL) — and the one thing that made them dangerous is gone: Yashin is off their lineup entirely, no line assignment. That guts their top end; what's left is Bates/Parrish/Kvasha, who are grindy (Parrish 85 check, Bates 94 draw) but not the kind of speed that punishes a mistake. We're 18-5 on ten straight, 7.5 a night. My job Monday is to not do something stupid, not to chase an edge.

Two things genuinely matter and both are already in place. First, their penalty kill is 2-for-57 — a 3.5% kill is the weakest edge we'll get all month, and our first power-play unit now has Gaborik on it (that was set this morning as a matchup call against exactly this). The instruction from here is simply to give that unit ice when we get it; no further personnel move helps against a kill that bad. Second, their faceoff centre Bates (94) will win it off Richards, Chlup and Spezza — but in this game the only lever I have is who centres, and I'm not pulling Sundin down to chase draws against a team that scores 2.5 a night. I'll live with losing the draw and winning the scoreboard.

What I'm deliberately **not** doing: throwing the surplus at them. We have four checkers at 90-plus, and I've said before the time to lean on them is against a hot offensive club, not a 2.5-goal team missing its best player. Deploying a shutdown look here would be me making a change to feel involved. We keep the lines that are winning.

Belfour starts Monday — cleared for the 5th, and he's the one goalie who doesn't blink in a road building. That's locked from the season plan, not a matchup tweak.

# Run 07 — assessment (in-game 2004-12-04)

Next: at NY Islanders, 2004-12-06. We sit 18-5-0 (147-76) on a ten-game
win streak; NYI are 12-10-1, 4-6 in their last ten, giving up 3.3 a game.

## Phase 1 — development

The club is deep and the kids are mostly getting real chances. The honest
read of who is earning and receiving, not who is developing (I have no
weeks-apart numbers to judge that):

**Getting his chance and taking it — no change.**
- Nash (20): 25 games, 22 pts, our most-iced young forward at 12.9 a night. Nothing to fix.
- Gaborik (22): 25 games, 34 pts, 18.4 a night on the second unit, just moved up to the first power play. Thriving.
- Chlup (18): 8 pts in 14 games on the third line, 11.1 a night. He came off the injured list Dec 3 and is straight back in the lineup — that is exactly the chance a high-ceiling kid at centre should get. Good.
- Klesla (22), Eminger (21), Upshall (21), Alexeev (22): all dress, all 13-15 mpg, all producing. No concerns.

**Under-iced for the numbers he is posting — this is my one real lever.**
- Koltsov (23): 12 pts in 11 games — the best points-per-game on this club (1.09) — and he is still only seeing 9.3 a night on the speed line. No injury row; this is usage, not health. He and Spezza and Alexeev make the line the club's fastest. I am not breaking a winning group, but a player that productive has to get more of the game. **Give that speed line more minutes**, that is the smaller intervention and it answers Koltsov (and Spezza) without pulling anyone off a line that is working.

**Worth keeping an eye on, not worth a forced change.**
- Spacek (19): 6 pts in 11 games at a heavy 16.0 a night, now off the dressing list with no injury behind it. That is a real step down for a kid who had earned those minutes. But he is a centre, and centre is Sundin, Richards, Spezza, Chlup — there is no clean slot. I flag it, I do not force it.
- Chistov (21): the scouting opinion on him is high (95) but he is not producing right now — 4 pts in 14 games — and he is scratched. Ceiling is not current ability; he is not out-earning any winger who dresses. He has to take a spot, not be given one. Not off my radar, but he is not owed a shift tonight.

**Not owed a roster spot for being young — said plainly.**
- Smirnov (19): zero games and a low scouting number (70). Nobody on this club is losing a shift so Smirnov can have one.
- Safronov (23): zero games, no path behind a healthy Colaiacovo on the back end. Stands from before.

**Bottom line for phase 1:** this is not a club that is starving its youth — the majority of the under-23 group dresses and produces. The single clean, no-cost development call is to run Koltsov's speed line more. Everything else is either already right, or not worth disturbing a ten-game winner to fix.


## Phase 2 — opponent matchup

NY Islanders, Dec 6 at their building. They are 12-10-1, and cold: 4-6 in
their last ten, 2.50 goals a game for, 3.30 against. Home/road is a wash
(8-5 at home, 3-6 OT away), so there is no trip factor to respect. This is
not a hot offensive club — it is a mid-table side leaking goals at 3.3 a
night. That matters for my one standing principle about the checking units:
I said I give our shutdown lines more of the game against a hot scorer, not
a 2.5-goal team. This is not that game.

We are 18-5-0, winners of ten straight, outscoring teams 75-18 over that
run. On merit this is a game we should win on our own terms. Nothing about
NYI forces a special-teams overhaul.

## Phase 3 — role composition / lines

The one composition fault worth a call is spending our right-side scorer on
the penalty kill. As of the current lineup, Gaborik (34 pts, third on the
club) is on the first kill unit with Roberts, Fischer and Colaiacovo. He is
a finisher, not a checker, and every shift he spends killing is a shift not
driving the offence that has us at 7.5 goals a game. We have plenty of
killers — Roberts and Fischer both check at 90-plus, Upshall and Richards
and McCabe and Kaberle are all capable, and Tucker/Svehla check at 92 as
extras. We do not need a 34-point forward eating PK minutes.

So:

- **Get Gaborik off the kill.** Use a genuine checker in his place (Roberts
  and Fischer stay; put Upshall or Richards up with them). Keep Gaborik on
  the power play where he belongs. Reason class: role-gap — I am short a
  checking body on the kill mid-game and I am spending a scorer to cover it.
  Confidence: high.
- **He belongs on the first power-play unit.** He is 34 points, right up
  with Sundin and McCabe and behind only Mogilny. On merit and as a hot
  right winger, that is first-unit company, not second. I would move him up
  onto the unit with Sundin and Mogilny. Reason class: development/merit.
  This is texture, not panic — the power play is not broken; I am just
  putting the better shooter on the first unit.
- **Goalie: Belfour, confirmed** for Dec 6. Both men are healthy and his
  season (2.57, .907) is clearly ahead of David's (3.24, .879). David gets
  the next one after, as promised. Reason class: matchup. No change from
  what we agreed.

I would not touch the even-strength lines — they are 10 straight and
chemistry is real. The speed line (Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev) carries my
development call from phase one: give it more of the game, because Koltsov
is producing at a point a game and only seeing 9.3 a night. That stays a
minutes call, not a line change.

## Final call for Dec 6

Two moves, both small, both aimed at the same thing — stop spending our
best skill on roles that do not use it:
1. Gaborik off the kill, on the first power play (role-gap + merit).
2. Belfour in net (matchup, reaffirmed).
Give Koltsov's line more of the game. Everything else holds on a ten-game
winner.

# 2004-12-04 — Run 05: NYI away, Dec 6

## Situation

Ten straight wins, 7.5 GF and 1.8 GA a game over the last ten (q36). NYI are 12-10, patchy lately, scoring 2.5 and allowing 3.3 a game over their last ten (q37). First meeting of the season (q31). We are the hotter club by a mile; the job is not to out-think them, it is to not fiddle with what works and to get the two small things right.

## Phase 1 — Development (U23, club has played 25)

Going player by player on "is he getting the games he has earned":

- **Gaborik (22)** — 25/25, 18.4 mpg, 34 pts. Fully earned and fully used. Rightfully on line 2; the only thing he's owed is power-play time — see below.
- **Nash (20)** — 25/25, 22 pts, third line at 12.9 mpg. Earning every shift he gets. No change.
- **Koltsov (23)** — 12 pts in 11 GP is 1.09 a game, and I checked: **no injury row for him anywhere** (q25 — the only injuries on file are Colaiacovo, Mogilny, Sundin, Belfour, Chlup). So this isn't the injury artifact I flagged before. He's healthy, he's on the fourth line, and he's at 9.3 mpg while producing at the club's best pace. He has earned more than this. **But** I will not crack a 10-game winning streak by re-stacking lines the night before a road game. The smaller tool: give the Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev line more of the game tonight — roll them against the other team's threes and fours, let Koltsov's hands pay the rent. Development + production, not matchup.
- **Chlup (18)** — 14 GP with a recent injury on file (returned Dec 3, q25); he's centering the third line at 11.1 mpg with 6 goals in that span. For an 18-year-old coming off a knock, that's the chance we talked about. Keep it.
- **Colaiacovo (21)** — 10 GP but 18.7 mpg when in on the second pair, and on both PP and PK units. The low GP share is a byproduct of a healthy top four on a winning team; his per-game trust is right.
- **Spezza, Upshall, Eminger, Klesla, Alexeev (21-22)** — 22-25 GP, real roles, all producing double-digit points except the checking work of Upshall/Eminger. All earned. No change.
- **Chistov (21)** — healthy (no injury row, q25), 4 pts in 14 GP, not dressing. A 21-year-old with our best scouting number on the wing watching from the stand. This was my call on Dec 4 and with ten straight wins I am not reversing it on the eve of a game, but he and Spacek are the first names in if anyone sags. Morale 90, so no damage yet — that is exactly the number I watch.
- **Spacek (19)** — 11 GP at 16 mpg, then off the dressing sheet since, healthy. Same verdict as Chistov: first in line, not tonight.
- **Smirnov (19) and Safronov (23)** — zero games. Smirnov is a project, fine. Safronov is a 23-year-old defenceman with a strong scouting number and no path through Kaberle, McCabe, Fischer, Eminger, Colaiacovo and Klesla. If he's still not dressing by the All-Star break, that's a roster question for the GM, not a coaching one.

**Development verdict: no line changes tonight.** Koltsov gets more of the game via usage, not via a shuffle. The young players who are playing are playing because they earned it; the two healthy scratches (Chistov, Spacek) are scratch because winning is, not because of anything they did.

## Phase 2 — Roles / Matchup vs NYI

- **Their top end is Jason Blake (33 pts) and Mark Parrish (29), with Hamrlik (28) and Aucoin (22) producing from the blue line** (q41). Hamrlik and Aucoin log 27-30 minute nights and join the rush — our first power-play unit needs to be what answers, because their penalty kill will see Sundin and Mogilny a lot.
- **Yashin is on their roster and 25 pts in 16 GP but has no line assignment** (q34 does not carry him; consistent with what I noted Dec 4). Treat him as not playing unless they surprise us; if he dresses, Roberts draws him and Sundin stays off the faceoff against him.
- Their checking centre is Bates (51% on 158 draws, q41). Richards centres our second line and can handle that without a specialist matchup change.
- **Our shutdown surplus stays benched one more night.** Tucker, Svehla, Fischer — we decided Dec 4 the fourth line is speed, not checking, and the last ten games (18 GA in 10) say the redress plan can wait for a day we're not rolling. This is a matchup choice, and I own it: against a 2.5-goal-a-night club, speed beats smothering.

## Phase 3 — Units and the goalie

- **Goalie: Belfour starts Monday night at NYI.** His name was on the injury list with a return date of Dec 5 (q25); that date has passed and he is the best thing we have — 2.57 GAA, .907, three shutouts (q32). Aebischer gets the promise, exactly as recorded: the next Toronto game after this one, Dec 7 at home vs NJ.
- **Power play, the one real change: Gaborik onto the first unit.** I decided this on Dec 4 and the unit as it stands still shows him on the second (q26 — P1 is Sundin/Roberts/Mogilny/McCabe/Kaberle). He is our leading scorer at 34 points; he belongs on the unit that takes the majority of the chances. Drop him in over Mogilny, who is a week back from a knock — Mogilny keeps the second unit. Reason class: production.
- **Penalty kill unchanged.** Fischer/Colaiacovo up front on the first kill, Roberts' hands on the 5-on-3 — none of it has given us a problem.
- **Lines unchanged.** Line 1: Sundin/Roberts/Mogilny. Line 2: Richards/Gaborik/Afinogenov. Line 3: Chlup/Nash/Upshall with Klesla/Eminger behind them. Line 4: Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev — **roll this line more than usual tonight.**

## To the GM

Belfour in net, Gaborik up to the first power-play unit, fourth line gets more ice. Nothing else moves.

## Sign-off

Phase 1 (development): done — no lineup changes; Koltsov via usage, Chistov/Spacek held as first-in, Safronov raised to the GM as a roster question.
Phase 2 (matchup): done — no line or PK changes; game plan built around Blake/Parrish and their QB rush; Yashin treated as a scratch.
Phase 3 (units/goalie): done — Belfour starts; Gaborik to PP1; Aebischer Dec 7.
Recommendations recorded: r1 (goalie), r2 (PP1), r3 (4th-line usage), r4 (no change), r5 (scratch hold), r6 (roster gap).

---

# Phase 2 — Roles

## Q1: Is each unit built from players who suit it?

Mostly yes, and I am not going to pretend otherwise to justify a busy night.

- **L1 (Sundin/Roberts/Mogilny, McCabe/Fischer)** — checking mean 79 with Fischer 90 and Roberts 90 behind elite scoring. Suit as is.
- **L2 (Richards/Gaborik/Afinogenov, Kaberle/Colaiacovo)** — checking mean 68, the softest of the top three. That's fine: it's our second scoring unit and it should be judged on the 84/93 scoring, not asked to smother anyone.
- **L3 (Chlup/Nash/Upshall, Klesla/Eminger)** — checking mean 79 built from Nash 83, Upshall 87, Eminger 83, Klesla 81 (q44). This is a genuine checking line wearing a third-line jersey. Exactly right.
- **L4 (Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev)** — speed mean 88, checking mean 60. That's the Dec 4 decision working: it is a speed line, not a checking line, and I will not ask it to be one. **But** the audit exposes its one real weakness: Spezza wins draws at 55 (q45) and nobody on that line can take a draw. I manage that with starts — Chlup's line (Chlup 75, best hands among the remaining centres) gets the Bates draws, Spezza's line is deployed away from the dot against NYI's top two.
- **P1 (Sundin/Roberts/Mogilny/McCabe/Kaberle)** — clutch mean 90/94, the right guys in the right spots. The addition of Gaborik (r2) is the only fix it needed; 17.9% on the season (5-for-28, q42) with this much talent says we needed another shot, not another system.
- **K1 (Roberts/Gaborik/Fischer/Colaiacovo)** — this is the one unit that does **not** suit. Our leading scorer is on the first penalty kill while two 92-checkers (Tucker, Svehla) watch from the press box. Fix below.
- **K2 (McCabe/Kaberle/Richards/Upshall)** — Kaberle is an offensive defenceman killing with the second unit; serviceable but it is the softest unit on the ice.

### The change that fixes both kill problems at once

We dress **six** defencemen — McCabe, Fischer, Kaberle, Colaiacovo, Klesla, Eminger (q26). Svehla is healthy (no injury row, q25) with the best defensive grading not in the lineup: checking 92, toughness 75, stamina 94 (q44). There is a seventh-defenceman slot sitting empty.

**Dress Svehla as the seventh defenceman. He replaces Gaborik on the first kill (with Fischer) and Kaberle on the second (with McCabe).** Nobody loses an even-strength job — the forward corps stays 12 deep untouched. Gaborik comes off the penalty kill entirely, which keeps his legs for the first power-play unit. Chemistry cost: one new defensive pairing on the kills; kills change combinations more than lines do and nobody's even-strength chemistry is touched. Reason class: **role-gap** — this is the first installment of the shutdown-surplus redress, taken at the smallest possible price.

Tucker stays scratched: we are 12 forwards deep and there is no forward spot to give him without benching someone who dresses and produces tonight. He is next in if a winger sags.

## Q2: Does the roster hold enough of each role?

- **Checking: surplus, not shortage.** Four guys at 89+ (Tucker 92, Svehla 92, Fischer 90, Roberts 90, McCabe 89 — q44). No shutdown pair we cannot build; the problem was never availability, it was usage. The Svehla move above starts draining the surplus.
- **Faceoff centres: this is the roster problem, and it is real.** The centres are Sundin 90, then a cliff — Chlup 75, Holden 71, Richards 70, Spezza 55 (q45). I have no centre who can reliably win a draw against another club's top line, and a fourth-line centre at 55 loses the dot to every third line in the league. **No arrangement of this roster fixes that.** If the GM goes looking before the trade deadline, the specific ask is a bottom-six centre who wins draws — a 78-85 faceoff man — not "more grit". We have all the grit anyone could want sitting undressed.
- **Toughness/enforcer: thin but I am not asking.** Best toughness on the roster is Roberts at 73. We are a speed and skill club on a ten-game streak; I would rather live with it than warp the identity, and the faceoff centre above likely brings some of it anyway.

---

# Phase 3 — Matchup: NYI, Monday Dec 6 (away)

## Honest read of them

23 games in, 12-10-1, and the last ten are the story: 2.5 scored, 3.3 allowed a night, 4-6 in that stretch (q37). Their season scoring (95 in 23) says they can put pucks in the net; the last month says they currently can't. Their top six is genuinely difficult — Bates centres a fast line with Kvasha and Parrish, and **Hamrlik and Aucoin are the dangerous part: 28 and 22 points from the blue line, shot power in the mid-90s, and both log huge nights** (q41). Their second and third pair — Niinimaa, Martinek, M. Timander, Hawgood — are mobile but every one of them carries an endurance grade in the low-to-mid 60s. That's the pressure point.

Two numbers I went and got because they change the plan:

- **Their power play is 2-for-57 — 3.5%, dead last in the league** (q46). Bates, Parrish, Hamrlik and Aucoin have the talent on the quarterdeck and none of it is converting. I am not going to build a defensive shell for an opponent who cannot score a man advantage in twenty-five attempts.
- **Our actual faceoff numbers are better than the grades fear**: Sundin is winning 73% (138 of 189), Richards 67%, Chlup 63%. Spezza is the one real liability at 32% (q48). Their Bates grades 94 on draws but sits at 51% actual (q41) — this cliff of ours is shallower in practice than on paper, and tonight it's manageable with deployment.

## What changes for Monday — and what doesn't

**Matchup reasons only here; the development calls (Koltsov's usage, Gaborik's points) stand on their own and are not dressed up as opponent prep.**

1. **No checking-line insertion.** My own redress plan says spend the Tucker/Svehla surplus against a *hot* offensive club. NYI is the opposite — 2.5 a night, cold for a month. Speed beats smothering here and the last ten games (18 GA in 10) back it. **Tucker stays home, and that is a matchup decision, not laziness.**
2. **Roll the speed at their bottom two pairs.** Gaborik/Afinogenov's line and Spezza/Koltsov/Alexeev get the majority of their shifts against Niinimaa/M. Timander and Hawgood — endurance grades in the low 60s, Hawgood 36 years old (brief). Our fourth line's speed mean of 88 is aimed straight at the 36-year-old. This is deployment, not composition — nobody changes jerseys.
3. **Faceoff deployment, not a faceoff specialist.** Chlup (63% actual) takes Bates and Scatchard; Sundin stays on Bates only when the first line's out there to change; **Spezza's line starts away from the dots** — at 32% I will not hand him a draw against anyone, let alone a club that needs a momentum goal.
4. **Penalty kill stays conservative but not panicked.** Their first unit is Bates/Kvasha/Parrish/Hamrlik/Aucoin — the shooting is real even if the conversion is the worst in the league. Box stays shell-lite: force it to the point men, nobody free-runs Bates through the middle. The Svehla addition from Phase 2 (role-gap) covers this nicely, and I'll take the credit overlap honestly — it's a better fit tonight because they can't kill us with it either way.
5. **Goalie: Belfour.** This is the matchup call — first road game of the streak, against a club desperate enough to press. His return date has passed and he's been our best netminder (2.57, .907, 3 SO — q32). Aebischer keeps his start Saturday vs NJ, promise intact. Their crease is the inverse: DiPietro has started 19 of 23 with rebound control graded 66 — if we get second chances on Long Island, they'll come cheap.
6. **Yashin watch.** Still unlined (q34). If he's somehow in theirs Monday, Roberts shadows him and Sundin avoids the draw against him. Otherwise it's noise.

## Verdict

Same four lines. Belfour in net. Speed on their bottom pairs, draws managed, nobody benched for a team scoring 2.5 a night. The streak travels.

---

## Final sign-off (all phases)

- Phase 1 — development: no lineup change; Koltsov via usage; Chistov/Spacek first-in; Safronov raised as roster question.
- Phase 2 — roles: Svehla in as seventh D, onto both kills; Gaborik off PK; faceoff-centre gap raised to GM; checking surplus, not shortage.
- Phase 3 — matchup: Belfour starts; no checking insertion (cold offence); speed rolled at bottom pairs; draws deployed around Spezza's 32%.
- Recommendations: r1 goalie, r2 PP1, r3 4th-line usage, r4 no-change lines, r5 scratch hold, r6 Safronov, r7 Svehla/PK, r8 faceoff-centre gap.
